explanation_text: On a dombra, pressing the string at a higher fret raises the note, just as a digit's position changes its value. A 3 in the tens place means 30, while a 3 in the hundreds place means 300.
image_prompt: Illustrate a dombra neck with frets labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how pressing higher up changes both the note and the value.

explanation_text: A cook sets out baursak on a platter and adds more as guests arrive, so the total rises. When guests take some away, the total falls—the same join-and-remove idea as addition and subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a platter of golden baursak being added to and taken from, with the changing count shown above it.

explanation_text: When one platter of beshbarmak is shared among several guests, multiplying finds the total and dividing splits it fairly. Twelve pieces shared by 4 guests gives each guest 3.
image_prompt: Show a beshbarmak platter being divided evenly among guests around a dastarkhan, each receiving an equal number of pieces.

explanation_text: Skewers of shashlik often hold meat in pairs, two pieces per group. When every piece finds a partner the count is even; one leftover piece makes the count odd.
image_prompt: Show shashlik skewers with meat pieces arranged in pairs, and one skewer with a single unmatched piece to show an odd number.

explanation_text: Traditional nauryz kozhe is made with seven ingredients, and cooks count them in sevens—7, 14, 21—as they fill pots for the festival. That rhythmic counting is skip counting.
image_prompt: Show seven ingredient bowls beside pots of nauryz kozhe, with the bowls counted in groups of seven.

explanation_text: The three lakes of the Altai range in Xinjiang sit at different mountain elevations, so their altitudes can be ordered from lowest to highest. Comparing them is like comparing numbers.
image_prompt: Show three mountain lakes of the Altai in Xinjiang at different altitudes with elevation labels and > and < symbols between them.

kazakh_culture: Estimating wool for a felt mat
explanation_text: A felt-maker estimates how much wool a mat needs by remembering the last mat she made, aiming for a close, convenient amount. That practical guesswork is estimation, like rounding to a nearby number.
image_prompt: Show a felt-maker weighing a pile of wool and estimating, with approximate kilogram amounts labeled nearby.

explanation_text: A full platter of beshbarmak is one whole, and each guest's portion is a fraction of it. Six guests sharing one platter each receive one sixth.
image_prompt: Show a beshbarmak platter divided into six equal sections, each labeled 1/6.

kazakh_culture: Halving a round nan, then quartering
explanation_text: Cut one round nan into two halves, or cut it into four quarters—both cuts give you the whole nan. Since 1/2 and 2/4 name the same amount, they are equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a round nan cut first into two halves and then into four quarters, with 1/2 and 2/4 labeled.

explanation_text: If the family has 8 sheep and 4 are white, the white sheep are 4/8 of the flock. Dividing top and bottom by 4 shows the same share more simply: 4/8 equals 1/2.
image_prompt: Show a flock of eight sheep with four white ones, labeled with 4/8 and 1/2.

explanation_text: A server offers three full bowls of kumis and one half-full bowl. Together that is 3½—a whole number joined to a fraction, called a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full bowls and one half-full bowl of kumis, labeled as 3½.

kazakh_culture: Shubat filling more than one bowl
explanation_text: When shubat fills one bowl and spills into a second, the same-size parts add up to more than one whole. A fraction like 5/4, where the top number is larger, is an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Show shubat filling one bowl and overflowing into a second, with four equal parts labeled 5/4.

explanation_text: The seven ingredients of nauryz kozhe go into the pot in measured parts. Adding three of the seven shares to four of the seven gives all seven—3/7 + 4/7 = 7/7, one full pot.
image_prompt: Show ingredient bowls pouring measured portions into a kozhe pot, with 3/7 + 4/7 = 7/7 labeled.

kazakh_culture: Pouring out part of the tea
explanation_text: A bowl of tea at the dastarkhan is filled to a fraction of its height and then partially shared out. What remains is the original fraction minus the poured portion.
image_prompt: Show a tea bowl with part of its contents poured out, the remaining amount labeled as a fraction of the full bowl.

kazakh_culture: Half of a half shashlik portion
explanation_text: Two friends split one skewer of shashlik, then one friend gives away half of their half. Half of a half is a quarter—exactly what multiplying fractions, 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, describes.
image_prompt: Show a shashlik skewer divided in half, with one half divided again, labeled 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

explanation_text: A sheet of baursak dough can be cut into strips and then into smaller squares. Counting how many of the small squares fit inside the whole sheet is like dividing a whole by a fraction.
image_prompt: Show a sheet of baursak dough being cut into equal squares, with the number of squares labeled.

explanation_text: At the bazaar, kumis is measured in liters, and the amounts fall between whole numbers. Halfway between one and two liters is 1.5 liters—decimals record those in-between amounts.
image_prompt: Show a measuring container marked 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters of kumis.

explanation_text: A bowl of shubat can be described as half a liter or as 0.5 liters. The fraction and the decimal name the very same amount, which is what converting between them means.
image_prompt: Show two containers holding the same amount, one marked ½ and the other 0.5.

kazakh_culture: Ripe apples in the Ili valley
explanation_text: An orchard in the Ili valley of Xinjiang, where many Kazakh farmers live, picks apples famous across the region. If 80 of every 100 apples picked are ripe, that is 80 percent—a way to count parts out of a hundred.
image_prompt: Show a crate of apples from an Ili valley orchard with 80 ripe ones labeled out of 100, with a large 80% mark.

explanation_text: A chapan marked 10% off drops its price by one tenth. Finding 10% of the original price shows how percents are used to find a part of a number.
image_prompt: Show a bazaar stall with a chapan on display and a sign reading 10% off next to the reduced price tag.

explanation_text: A host sets the table before knowing how many guests will arrive, planning portions around an unknown number x. The unknown quantity stands for a number to be found later—a variable.
image_prompt: Show a dastarkhan table being set, with a placeholder x over one seat and empty bowls awaiting guests.

kazakh_culture: Silk Road loads, known and unknown
explanation_text: A caravan carries two known bales of silk and an unknown number of additional bales, x. That situation can be written as 2 + x, a mathematical expression.
image_prompt: Show two loaded camels plus an unlabeled third camel, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: When the two pans of a trader's balance weigh exactly the same, the beam sits level. Two amounts being equal is the heart of an equation, where the two sides balance.
image_prompt: Show a balance scale with equal sacks on both pans, the beam level and labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: If one saddlebag is heavier, the rider removes a sack or shifts it until both sides match. One simple move restores the balance—just like solving a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a pack horse with uneven saddlebags and a rider removing one sack to make the load even.

explanation_text: Making tea takes two ordered steps: first bring the water to a boil, then pour it over the leaves. Solving a two-step equation likewise needs two operations in the right order.
image_prompt: Show the tea sequence—boiling water first, then adding it to a teapot—with two labeled steps.

explanation_text: One family's herd may hold more animals than a neighbor's. Stating which is larger or smaller is an inequality, written with a greater-than or less-than sign.
image_prompt: Show two herds of different sizes on the steppe with the > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: Beshbarmak follows a fixed order: the meat must simmer before the rolled dough is dropped in. Because the steps cannot be swapped, cooking it mirrors the fixed order of math operations.
image_prompt: Show the beshbarmak cooking sequence in labeled steps—simmering meat, then adding dough—in a fixed order.

kazakh_culture: Swapping an equal measure of milk
explanation_text: If a recipe calls for two liters of mare's milk, two liters of cow's milk works the same in the dish. Replacing an amount with an equal amount is substitution, like putting a number in place of a variable.
image_prompt: Show two containers of milk being swapped at equal measure, with a substitution arrow linking them.

explanation_text: Each star over the steppe marks one exact place in the sky. In geometry, a point marks a single location with no size—every shape is built from points.
image_prompt: Show a starry sky above the steppe with individual stars marked as dots on a faint grid.

explanation_text: From the shanyrak at the top of a yurt, the straight uyq poles fan out to the wall. Each pole is a straight line extending from the center toward the outside.
image_prompt: Show the interior of a yurt with uyq poles radiating from the crown like straight lines.

explanation_text: A yurt door swings open on its frame, and the gap between door and frame widens. The amount of that opening is an angle, measured in degrees.
image_prompt: Show a yurt door partially open with the angle between the door and frame clearly marked.

kazakh_culture: Right angles in the kerege lattice
explanation_text: The crossed wooden struts of the kerege wall meet at right angles. Those 90-degree crossings give the yurt its strength—perpendicular lines meeting square to each other.
image_prompt: Show the kerege lattice with crossing struts, one crossing highlighted with a 90° square.

explanation_text: Within each section of the kerege, struts run side by side and never touch. They stay an equal distance apart along their length—the definition of parallel lines.
image_prompt: Show the kerege lattice with two struts marked as parallel, running side by side without meeting.

explanation_text: A syrmak felt carpet is pieced from bold colored shapes with straight sides. Squares, triangles, and other closed many-sided figures are polygons.
image_prompt: Show a syrmak carpet built from square, triangular, and other polygon-shaped felt pieces.

explanation_text: Two neighboring uyq poles and the shanyrak rim frame a triangle in the roof. The yurt's round roof is ringed by these triangles, each with three sides.
image_prompt: Show the yurt roof from below, with one triangle highlighted between two poles and the crown.

explanation_text: When the kerege lattice stretches open, its crossings frame four-sided diamond cells. Each cell is a quadrilateral—a rhombus that flexes as the lattice folds and unfolds.
image_prompt: Show a section of the kerege lattice with one diamond-shaped cell highlighted and labeled.

explanation_text: Yurts at a camp are set in a ring, and walking the whole way around measures the ring's distance. That distance around the outside of a shape is its perimeter.
image_prompt: Show people walking around a ring of yurts with a dashed line tracing their path around the camp.

kazakh_culture: Felt rug covering the yurt floor
explanation_text: A felt rug spreads over a section of the yurt's round floor. The amount of floor the rug covers is its area, measured in squares of the floor.
image_prompt: Show a yurt interior with a felt rug covering part of the floor, the covered region shaded.

explanation_text: Kanas Lake in the Altai mountains of Xinjiang holds a vast amount of water in its deep basin. The space a three-dimensional body fills or can contain is its volume.
image_prompt: Show the deep blue waters of Kanas Lake with a measuring scale showing its volume.

explanation_text: Looking up inside a yurt, the shanyrak is a perfect circle with the roof poles meeting its rim. Its center, radius, and diameter can all be seen in one glance.
image_prompt: Show the shanyrak viewed from below, with radius and diameter lines drawn across the circle.

kazakh_culture: Round nan and the constant pi
explanation_text: Bakers shape round nan, and every circle relates its distance around to its distance across. Dividing a nan's circumference by its diameter always gives pi, about 3.14.
image_prompt: Show a round nan with a tape along its edge and a line across its middle, labeled circumference and diameter.

kazakh_culture: Rows and columns of the orchard
explanation_text: Apple trees in the Ili valley of Xinjiang are planted in straight rows and columns, so every tree has a row and a position in that row. A coordinate plane uses the same idea to place every point with two numbers.
image_prompt: Show an apple orchard in the Ili valley from above, trees in rows and columns, with row and column axes labeled.

kazakh_culture: Plotting yurts on a camp map
explanation_text: A sketched map of a camp marks where each family's yurt stands. Locating a yurt by distance across and distance along the camp is plotting a point.
image_prompt: Show a camp map with yurts marked as dots, each labeled with its coordinates.

explanation_text: Kazakh ornament often places the same horn curve on both sides of a center line. Folding along that line makes the two halves match—reflection symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a Kazakh oyu-örnek motif with a center line and both mirrored halves highlighted.

explanation_text: A single horn motif can be turned around a point and placed again at a new angle. Turning, sliding, or flipping a figure without changing its size is a transformation.
image_prompt: Show one Kazakh ornament motif repeated in rotated positions around a central point.

kazakh_culture: The two strings of the dombra
explanation_text: A dombra's two strings—one thicker, one thinner—produce different notes because their thicknesses compare in a fixed way. Comparing two quantities by division is a ratio.
image_prompt: Show a dombra close-up with its two strings labeled with a thickness ratio like 2:1.

explanation_text: To make a larger syrmak, a craftsperson copies a small design while keeping every part in the same relation. When the ratios stay equal at every size, the drawing is in proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small syrmak design and a larger copy side by side, with matching shapes at both sizes.

explanation_text: In a baiga, a long-distance horse race, riders compare how far each horse travels in the same time. Distance per hour, a rate for one hour, is a unit rate.
image_prompt: Show a baiga race across the steppe with a label reading kilometers per hour.

explanation_text: Old maps shrank the long Silk Road through Xinjiang to fit on parchment, with a rule such as one finger-length equals one day's ride. A drawing that keeps real distances proportional at a smaller size is a scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show an old map of the Silk Road through Xinjiang beside a caravan, with a scale legend marked.

explanation_text: A berkutchi (eagle hunter) records how many hunts succeed each month. If successes rise from 40 to 48, that is an increase of 8, or 20%—a percent change.
image_prompt: Show a berkutchi's hunting journal with monthly tallies rising from 40 to 48 and a +20% label.

kazakh_culture: Tallying the herd at spring count
explanation_text: Each spring a family counts its animals, herd by herd, marking horses, sheep, goats, and camels. Writing down these counts is data collection.
image_prompt: Show a herder making tally marks on a board while counting sheep and horses.

explanation_text: A caravan master records each day's travel in a table of days and distances. Such a table gathers numbers together so they can be compared and read at a glance.
image_prompt: Show a caravan resting at dusk beside a table listing day numbers and distance traveled.

explanation_text: To judge a good harvest, an orchard keeper adds the apples from several trees and divides by the number of trees. The fair share each tree contributes is the mean.
image_prompt: Show apple crates beside trees with a calculation adding their counts and dividing by the tree count.

kazakh_culture: Middle altitude of the Kanas lakes
explanation_text: Lining up the three lakes of the Altai range in Xinjiang by elevation, the middle one sits between the other two. That middle value is the median of the three altitudes.
image_prompt: Show the three lakes of the Altai in Xinjiang arranged by altitude with the middle lake highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: Among the horses of a herd, some coat colors appear more often than others. The color that appears most frequently is the mode of the data.
image_prompt: Show a herd of horses in several colors with the most common color shown as the largest group.

explanation_text: The lakes of the Altai range in Xinjiang climb the mountain, so their altitudes differ widely. Subtracting the lowest altitude from the highest gives the range of the data.
image_prompt: Show the highest and lowest lake of the Altai in Xinjiang marked on a mountain slope with the difference labeled as the range.

explanation_text: At a folk games celebration, each event—kokpar, archery, tug-of-war—earns a village a number of wins. Bar heights make those numbers easy to compare.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph where each bar is labeled with a national game and its number of wins.

kazakh_culture: Kokpar team points across the season
explanation_text: A kokpar team's points from round to round form a trail across the season. Joining the points with a line shows where the team rose or fell.
image_prompt: Show a line graph of kokpar team points plotted across the rounds of a tournament.

explanation_text: Nauryz kozhe blends seven ingredients, and each has its own share of the pot. A pie chart shows how the whole pot splits into those parts.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart with seven labeled slices, one for each ingredient of nauryz kozhe.

explanation_text: A berkutchi can tell from past hunts how often the eagle succeeds. If 6 of every 10 hunts succeed, the chance of success is 6/10—a probability.
image_prompt: Show a golden eagle on a hunter's arm with a count of successful hunts labeled 6 out of 10.

explanation_text: Felt carpets repeat the same curved horn motif across their surface in a steady rhythm. A design that repeats in a predictable order is a pattern.
image_prompt: Show a felt carpet covered in a repeating horn motif, with the repeated unit outlined.

explanation_text: If each guest is served three baursak, then the number of baursak is always three times the number of guests. Each guest count leads to exactly one total—an input-output rule called a function.
image_prompt: Show a platter of baursak with guests at a table, a diagram linking each guest to three baursak.
